claim: Layer 2/3 pyramidal neurons from human temporal cortex have a specific membrane capacitance (Cm) of ~0.5 µF/cm².
source: Here we show that layer 2/3 pyramidal neurons from human temporal cortex (HL2/3 PCs) have a specific membrane capacitance (Cm) of ~0.5 µF/cm2
evidence: Supported by experimental data from voltage transient fitting (Figure 1) and nucleated patch experiments (Figure 2)

claim: The specific membrane capacitance of ~0.5 µF/cm² in human L2/3 pyramidal neurons is half of the commonly accepted 'universal' value (~1 µF/cm²) for biological membranes.
source: layer 2/3 pyramidal neurons from human temporal cortex (HL2/3 PCs) have a specific membrane capacitance (Cm) of ~0.5 µF/cm2, half of the commonly accepted 'universal' value (~1 µF/cm2) for biological membranes.
evidence: Comparison between measured human Cm values and established literature values for biological membranes

claim: Low Cm value (~0.5 µF/cm²) significantly enhances synaptic charge-transfer from dendrites to soma in human L2/3 pyramidal neurons.
source: Models of 3D reconstructed HL2/3 PCs demonstrated that such low Cm value significantly enhances both synaptic charge-transfer from dendrites to soma and spike propagation along the axon.
evidence: Demonstrated through computational modeling of 3D reconstructed neurons with different Cm values (Figure 3a)

claim: Low Cm value (~0.5 µF/cm²) significantly enhances spike propagation along the axon in human L2/3 pyramidal neurons.
source: Models of 3D reconstructed HL2/3 PCs demonstrated that such low Cm value significantly enhances both synaptic charge-transfer from dendrites to soma and spike propagation along the axon.
evidence: Demonstrated through computational modeling showing increased propagation velocity (Figure 3c)

claim: This is the first demonstration that human cortical neurons have distinctive membrane properties.
source: This is the first demonstration that human cortical neurons have distinctive membrane properties, suggesting important implications for signal processing in human neocortex.
evidence: Authors' assertion based on their novel findings and comparison with existing literature

claim: The advanced cognitive capabilities of the human brain are often attributed to our recently evolved neocortex.
source: The advanced cognitive capabilities of the human brain are often attributed to our recently evolved neocortex.
evidence: Statement based on established scientific consensus

claim: It is not known whether the basic building blocks of the human neocortex, the pyramidal neurons, possess unique biophysical properties that might impact on cortical computations.
source: However, it is not known whether the basic building blocks of the human neocortex, the pyramidal neurons, possess unique biophysical properties that might impact on cortical computations.
evidence: Statement of knowledge gap in the field at the time of study

claim: The human cortex is thicker than rodent cortex, particularly layer 2/3.
source: Comparison of human and rodents cortices shows that the human cortex is thicker (in particular layer 2/3 [DeFelipe et al., 2002; Elston et al., 2001])
evidence: Supported by citations to previous anatomical studies

claim: The human cortex contains more white matter than rodent cortex.
source: Comparison of human and rodents cortices shows that the human cortex is thicker (in particular layer 2/3 [DeFelipe et al., 2002; Elston et al., 2001]), contains more white matter (Herculano-Houzel et al., 2010)
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study

claim: Human cortical neurons are larger than rodent cortical neurons.
source: Comparison of human and rodents cortices shows that the human cortex is thicker (in particular layer 2/3 [DeFelipe et al., 2002; Elston et al., 2001]), contains more white matter (Herculano-Houzel et al., 2010), its neurons are larger (Mohan et al., 2015)
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study

claim: Human cortical pyramidal cells have more synaptic connections per cell (15,000–30,000 for layer 2/3 pyramidal neurons) than rodent pyramidal cells.
source: its cortical pyramidal cells have more synaptic connections per cell (15,000–30,000 for layer 2/3 pyramidal neurons [DeFelipe, 2011; DeFelipe et al., 2002])
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies

claim: The human neocortex, and especially its neurons, is anatomically unique.
source: It seems that the human neocortex, and especially its neurons, is anatomically unique.
evidence: Inference drawn from the anatomical differences described in the preceding sentences

claim: Specific membrane capacitance and cable characteristics are key in determining information processing in neurons and in the networks they form.
source: These have been shown to be key in determining information processing in neurons and in the networks they form (Segev and Rall, 1988; Major et al., 1994; Stuart and Spruston, 1998; Magee, 1998; Segev and London, 2000; Poirazi and Mel, 2001; London and Häusser, 2005; Hay et al., 2011; Eyal et al., 2014; Markram et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to previous studies

claim: Detailed 3D cable and compartmental models of L2/3 pyramidal cells from the human temporal cortex were built based on in vitro intracellular physiological and anatomical data.
source: To probe the biophysical properties of cortical neurons we built detailed 3D cable and compartmental models of L2/3 pyramidal cells from the human temporal cortex (HL2/3 PCs). The models were based on in vitro intracellular physiological and anatomical data from these same cells.
evidence: Description of the methodology used in the study

claim: Fresh cortical tissue was obtained from brain operations at the neurosurgical department in Amsterdam.
source: To collect this data, fresh cortical tissue was obtained from brain operations at the neurosurgical department in Amsterdam.
evidence: Description of experimental procedures

claim: The models of human neurons incorporate data on dendritic spines obtained from light-microscope studies in HL2/3 PCs.
source: Our models of human neurons also incorporate data on dendritic spines obtained from light-microscope studies in HL2/3 PCs (Benavides-Piccione et al., 2013; DeFelipe et al., 2002; Elston et al., 2001).
evidence: Description of model construction with citations to data sources

claim: These are the first-ever detailed models of human neurons.
source: These are the first-ever detailed models of human neurons.
evidence: Authors' assertion about the novelty of their work

claim: The best fit between experimental and theoretical voltage transients was obtained with Cm = 0.45 μF/cm² for the cell shown in Figure 1a.
source: The green transient (with Ra = 203 Ωcm, Rm = 38,907 Ωcm2 and Cm = 0.45 μF/cm2) best fitted the experimental transient.
evidence: Demonstrated by fitting model to experimental data in Figure 1a

claim: Attempts to fit the experimental transient with larger values of Cm failed.
source: Attempts to fit the transient with larger values of Cm failed (red and magenta traces).
evidence: Shown by poor fits with higher Cm values in Figure 1a

claim: The low value for Cm, around 0.5 μF/cm², was found in all six modeled human L2/3 pyramidal cells.
source: Furthermore, the low value for Cm, around 0.5 μF/cm2, was found in all these five additional modeled cells (Cm= 0.47 ± 0.03 μF/cm2, mean ± S.D, n = 6).
evidence: Quantitative results from fitting six different cells

claim: The RMSD obtained with Cm = 0.5 µF/cm² is much smaller than the one obtained with larger Cm values.
source: In all cases, the RMSD obtained with Cm = 0.5 µF/cm2 is much smaller than the one obtained with the larger Cm value (Figure 1—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: Demonstrated by RMSD analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1b

claim: The value of Ra has a negligible impact on the RMSD.
source: whereas the value of Ra has a negligible impact on the RMSD (Figure 1—figure supplement 1d).
evidence: Shown by RMSD analysis in Figure 1—figure supplement 1d

claim: The prediction of low Cm value in human L2/3 pyramidal neurons holds independently of the Ra value chosen.
source: However, we would like to re-emphasize that our prediction of low Cm value in human L2/3 pyramidal neurons holds independently of the Ra value chosen (Figure 1—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: Demonstrated by analysis showing Cm estimation is independent of Ra

claim: Even with large systematic errors in morphological parameters, the best fit still yields low Cm value in human L2/3 pyramidal neurons.
source: We found that even with large systematic errors in morphological parameters, the best fit still yields low Cm value in human L2/3 pyramidal neurons (see Table 1).
evidence: Error analysis results presented in Table 1

claim: The low Cm value ~ 0.5 μF/cm² found in HL2/3 PCs is surprising.
source: The low Cm value ~ 0.5 μF/cm2 found in HL2/3 PCs is surprising
evidence: Authors' interpretation of their findings in context of existing knowledge

claim: It is commonly assumed that Cm is close to 1 μF/cm².
source: it is commonly assumed that Cm is close to 1 μF/cm2 (Hodgkin et al., 1952; Cole, 1968)
evidence: Statement of established scientific consensus with citations

claim: Cm close to 1 μF/cm² was modeled by many researchers on rodent neurons.
source: as was modeled by many researchers on rodent neurons (Major et al., 1994; Roth and Häusser, 2001; Nörenberg et al., 2010; Szoboszlay et al., 2016)
evidence: Supported by citations to previous modeling studies

claim: Cm close to 1 μF/cm² was directly confirmed for several classes of neurons using patch recordings from nucleated membrane patches.
source: and directly confirmed for several classes of neurons using patch recordings from nucleated membrane patches (Gentet et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous experimental study

claim: The best theoretical fit to the experimental transients in mouse L2/3 PCs yields Cm of 1.09 ± 0.36 µF/cm².
source: In contrast to human neurons, and in agreement with the existing literature, we found that the best theoretical fit to the experimental transients yields Cm of 1.09 ± 0.36 µF/cm2 (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Experimental data from fitting mouse neuron models (n=4)

claim: The Cm value in mouse L2/3 neurons (1.09 ± 0.36 µF/cm²) is significantly larger compared to that found in human L2/3 neurons.
source: This value is significantly larger compared to that found in Figure 1 for human L2/3 neurons (students t-test without the assumption of equal variance, p-val = 0.0408, non parametric Mann-Whitney U-test, p-val = 0.0095).
evidence: Statistical comparison between human and mouse data

claim: The low value of Cm in human neurons is associated with a high Rm.
source: It is important to note that the low value of Cm in human neurons is associated with a high Rm
evidence: Observation from the fitted model parameters

claim: The membrane time constant (τm = Cm*Rm) in human L2/3 pyramidal neurons is in the range of 10–22 ms (τm = 16.5 ± 3.7, n = 6).
source: such that the membrane time constant (τm = Cm*Rm) is in the range of 10–22 ms (τm = 16.5 ± 3.7, n = 6)
evidence: Calculated from measured Cm and Rm values

claim: The membrane time constant in human L2/3 pyramidal neurons is similar to the value found in mouse L2/3 pyramidal neurons (τm = 16.1 ± 1.3, n = 4).
source: which is similar to the value found in the mouse L2/3 pyramidal neurons (τm = 16.1 ± 1.3, n = 4)
evidence: Comparison of calculated time constants between species

claim: The membrane time constant in human L2/3 pyramidal neurons is similar to that in rat L2/3 pyramidal cells (τm = 13.1 ± 1.7).
source: and in rat L2/3 pyramidal cells (τm = 13.1 ± 1.7, [Sarid et al., 2007]).
evidence: Comparison with published data from rat neurons

claim: The temporal resolution (the synaptic integration time-window) of human and rodents' pyramidal L2/3 cells is similar.
source: This implies that the temporal resolution (the synaptic integration time-window) of human and rodents' pyramidal L2/3 cells is similar.
evidence: Inference from the similar membrane time constants

claim: Non-uniform distribution of Rm in the dendrites was examined as a possible factor affecting Cm estimation.
source: Perhaps non-uniform distribution of Rm in the dendrites (as was shown in rodent layer 5 PCs [Stuart and Spruston, 1998] and in inhibitory basket cells [Nörenberg et al., 2010]), or active membrane currents such as Ih that are open around the resting membrane potential (Kole et al., 2006; Harnett et al., 2015), affect our estimation for Cm? These two possibilities were examined via simulations.
evidence: Description of additional simulations performed to test alternative hypotheses

claim: The estimated Cm for the optimal non-uniform Rm case was similar to the value obtained when Rm was uniform.
source: In all six cases the estimated Cm for the optimal non-uniform case was similar to the value obtained when Rm was uniform (not shown).
evidence: Results from simulations with non-uniform Rm

claim: The larger the Ih density, the larger was the estimated Cm value that best fitted the experimental transient.
source: We found that the larger the Ih density, the larger was the estimated Cm value that best fitted the experimental transient (from ~0.45 μF/cm2 without Ih, Figure 1—figure supplement 3a1, to ~0.76 μF/cm2 when Ih density at the soma was 0.2 mS/cm2, as found in rat L5PC (Kole et al., 2006), Figure 1—figure supplement 3c1).
evidence: Results from simulations with varying Ih densities

claim: The quality of the fit was significantly reduced with Ih compared to the passive case, particularly at short times.
source: However, the quality of the fit was significantly reduced compared to the passive case particularly at short times (Figure 1—figure supplement 3b2,c2).
evidence: Comparison of fit quality with and without Ih shown in supplementary figures

claim: In the first few milliseconds, the voltage transient is dominated by the capacitive membrane current (and not by the ionic currents, e.g., Ih).
source: Indeed, in the first few milliseconds, the voltage transient is dominated by the capacitive membrane current (and not by the ionic currents, e.g., Ih)
evidence: Based on understanding of membrane biophysics and circuit theory

claim: At short times, a close match between model and experiments was obtained only with Cm ~ 0.5 μF/cm², even in the presence of Ih.
source: at these short times, a close match between model and experiments was obtained only with Cm ~ 0.5 μF/cm2, even in the presence of Ih (Figure 1—figure supplement 3d1).
evidence: Results from simulations with Ih constrained to Cm = 0.5 μF/cm²

claim: In order to explain the experimental transients in human L2/3 neurons, Cm should be ~0.5 μF/cm².
source: We therefore conclude that in order to explain the experimental transients in human L2/3 neurons, Cm should be ~0.5 μF/cm2.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the modeling and simulation results

claim: Nucleated patch experiments were performed to directly measure Cm in HL2/3 PCs.
source: This puzzling result of low Cm, values in human neurons inspired us to perform a new set of experiments, using nucleated patches from HL2/3 PCs, in order to directly measure Cm, exactly as in Gentet et al. (2000).
evidence: Description of experimental methodology

claim: Nucleated patch experiments yielded an experimental value for Cm of 0.51 ± 0.11 μF/cm² in human L2/3 neurons (n = 5 neurons).
source: We obtained an experimental value for Cm of 0.51 ± 0.11 μF/cm2 (mean ± S.D, n = 5 neurons, see details on these cells in Table 2), in full agreement with our model prediction (Figure 2).
evidence: Direct experimental measurements from nucleated patches

claim: The nucleated patch Cm measurement in human neurons is in full agreement with the model prediction.
source: We obtained an experimental value for Cm of 0.51 ± 0.11 μF/cm2 (mean ± S.D, n = 5 neurons, see details on these cells in Table 2), in full agreement with our model prediction (Figure 2).
evidence: Comparison between model predictions and direct measurements

claim: Nucleated patch experiments in mouse neurons resulted in a Cm of 0.83 ± 0.34 μF/cm² (n = 7 neurons from 7 mice).
source: Repeating the same procedure in mouse neurons resulted in a Cm of 0.83 ± 0.34 μF/cm2 (n = 7 neurons from 7 mice; Figure 2d)
evidence: Direct experimental measurements from mouse nucleated patches

claim: The mouse Cm value from nucleated patches is similar to the findings of Gentet et al. (2000) and Szoboszlay et al. (2016).
source: Repeating the same procedure in mouse neurons resulted in a Cm of 0.83 ± 0.34 μF/cm2 (n = 7 neurons from 7 mice; Figure 2d), similar to the findings of (Gentet et al., 2000; Szoboszlay et al., 2016)
evidence: Comparison with published values from other studies

claim: The mouse Cm value from nucleated patches is significantly different from the human Cm values (p-val = 0.0472).
source: and significantly different from the human Cm values (students t-test following the KS test for normality (Massey, 1951), p-val = 0.0472).
evidence: Statistical comparison between human and mouse nucleated patch data

claim: Combining both methods (model fittings and nucleated patches), human Cm = 0.49 ± 0.08 μF/cm² (n = 11) and mouse Cm = 0.93 ± 0.36 μF/cm² (n = 11).
source: Combining the Cm values obtained in both methods, the model fittings (Figure 1) and the nucleated patches (Figure 2) shows the large difference in Cm between human (Cm = 0.49 ± 0.08 μF/cm2, n = 11) and mouse (Cm = 0.93 ± 0.36 μF/cm2, n = 11).
evidence: Combined analysis of all experimental data from both methods

claim: The difference in Cm between human and mouse is highly significant (p-val = 0.0021 by t-test, p-val = 0.006 by Mann-Whitney U-test).
source: This difference is highly significant (Figure 2d, students t-test following the KS test for normality, p-val = 0.0021, non-parametric Mann-Whitney U-test, p-val = 0.006).
evidence: Statistical analysis of combined human and mouse data

claim: Human L2/3 pyramidal neurons have different membrane capacitance compared to that of rodent pyramidal neurons.
source: Thus, we find that human L2/3 pyramidal neurons have different membrane capacitance compared to that of rodent pyramidal neurons.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the combined experimental evidence

claim: The peak somatic EPSP is larger by ~84% (basal synapse) to ~93% (apical synapse) when Cm = 0.45 μF/cm² compared to Cm = 0.9 μF/cm².
source: We found that the peak somatic excitatory postsynaptic potential (EPSP) is larger by ~84% (basal synapse) to ~93% (apical synapse) when Cm = 0.45 μF/cm2 (red traces) as compared to the case with Cm = 0.9 μF/cm2 (blue traces).
evidence: Computational modeling results shown in Figure 3a

claim: The dendritic delay from the distal tuft synapse was dramatically reduced from 39 ms when Cm = 0.9 μF/cm² to 20 ms when Cm = 0.45 μF/cm².
source: The dendritic delay from the distal tuft and basal synapses was dramatically reduced from 39 ms and 11 ms when Cm = 0.9 μF/cm2 to 20 ms and 6.5 ms respectively, when Cm = 0.45 μF/cm2
evidence: Computational modeling results comparing dendritic delays

claim: The dendritic delay from the distal basal synapse was dramatically reduced from 11 ms when Cm = 0.9 μF/cm² to 6.5 ms when Cm = 0.45 μF/cm².
source: The dendritic delay from the distal tuft and basal synapses was dramatically reduced from 39 ms and 11 ms when Cm = 0.9 μF/cm2 to 20 ms and 6.5 ms respectively, when Cm = 0.45 μF/cm2
evidence: Computational modeling results comparing dendritic delays

claim: With Cm = 0.45 μF/cm², about 100 excitatory synapses were required for generating a somatic spike with 50% probability.
source: With Cm = 0.45 μF/cm2, about 100 excitatory synapses were required for generating a somatic spike with 50% probability
evidence: Computational modeling results shown in Figure 3b

claim: With Cm = 0.9 μF/cm², about 170 synapses were required for generating a somatic spike with 50% probability.
source: whereas about 170 synapses were required with Cm = 0.9 μF/cm2.
evidence: Computational modeling results shown in Figure 3b

claim: The lower Cm value as found in HL2/3 pyramidal cells both improved synaptic charge transfer from dendrites to soma and also reduced the number of synapses required to initiate a somatic/axonal spike.
source: The lower Cm value as found in HL2/3 pyramidal cells both improved synaptic charge transfer from dendrites to soma (larger EPSPs and reduced dendritic delay) and also reduced the number of synapses required to initiate a somatic/axonal spike
evidence: Summary of computational modeling results from Figure 3

claim: Lower Cm compensates for the increase in the size of the dendritic tree in human neocortex.
source: thus compensating for the increase in the size of the dendritic tree in human neocortex (Mohan et al., 2015).
evidence: Inference from modeling results combined with anatomical data

claim: A lower Cm value increased the propagation speed of the action potential along the axon.
source: As expected, a lower Cm value increased the propagation speed of the action potential
evidence: Computational modeling results shown in Figure 3c

claim: For the parameters used, spike propagation was about 65% faster with lower Cm compared with the case of a higher Cm.
source: for the parameters we used, the propagation was about 65% faster compared with the case of a higher Cm.
evidence: Quantitative result from axonal spike propagation modeling in Figure 3c

claim: The modeling result on spike propagation velocity is in agreement with the analytical result obtained by Jack et al. (1975) for the impact of Cm on spike propagation velocity.
source: This is in agreement with the analytical result obtained by (Jack et al., 1975, page 432) for the impact of Cm on spike propagation velocity.
evidence: Comparison with theoretical predictions from cable theory

claim: Low Cm value enables an efficient intra- and inter-regional information-transfer despite the large size of the human brain.
source: Thus, low Cm value enables an efficient intra- and inter-regional information-transfer despite the large size of the human brain.
evidence: Inference from the modeling results on spike propagation and synaptic integration

claim: This study provides the first direct evidence for the unique properties of the membrane in human cortical cells.
source: Our study provides the first direct evidence for the unique properties of the membrane in human cortical cells.
evidence: Authors' summary of their contribution

claim: A few studies have demonstrated that Cm in rodent's pyramidal neurons may range between 0.7–2 µF/cm².
source: It is important to note that a few studies have demonstrated that Cm in rodent's pyramidal neurons may range between 0.7–2 µF/cm2 (Major et al., 1994; Thurbon et al., 1998)
evidence: Summary of previous literature findings

claim: Direct measurements using nucleated patches found a much narrower range of Cm, 0.8–1.1 µF/cm², in cortical pyramidal neurons.
source: but direct measurements using nucleated patches found a much narrower range, 0.8–1.1 µF/cm2, in cortical pyramidal neurons (Gentet et al., 2000; Szoboszlay et al., 2016), as well as in cerebellar Golgi cells (Szoboszlay et al., 2016).
evidence: Summary of previous experimental findings

claim: The narrow range of Cm values (0.8–1.1 µF/cm²) agrees with the modeling prediction of Nörenberg et al. (2010) for GABAergic hippocampal interneurons.
source: This narrow range of values also agrees with the modeling prediction of (Nörenberg et al., 2010) for GABAergic hippocampal interneurons, where a correction for the spines area is not required.
evidence: Comparison with previous modeling study

claim: Both a modeling approach and nucleated patch experiments were used to demonstrate that Cm in human L2/3 pyramidal neurons is significantly lower than in rodents.
source: In the present work, we used both a modeling approach, as well as nucleated patch experiments, to demonstrate that Cm in human L2/3 pyramidal neurons is significantly lower than in rodents.
evidence: Summary of the methodological approach and main finding

claim: The neurons used originated from humans with epileptic seizures.
source: One may argue that the neurons we used have abnormal membrane properties as these neurons originated from humans with epileptic seizures.
evidence: Description of the patient population

claim: Only brain samples that were not part of the diseased tissues were used.
source: However, we only used brain samples that were not part of the diseased tissues, but had to be removed in order to gain access to deeper brain structures for surgical treatment.
evidence: Description of tissue selection criteria

claim: The eleven HL2/3 pyramidal cells used were taken from five different human patients with different disease records that were treated with different drugs.
source: The eleven HL2/3 pyramidal cells used in this research (six cells in Figure 1 and five cells in Figure 2) were taken from five different human patients with different disease records that were treated with different drugs (see Table 2).
evidence: Description of the sample diversity

claim: In all cases (across five different patients), similar membrane properties were found.
source: Yet, in all cases we found similar membrane properties.
evidence: Consistency of findings across different patients

claim: There is no correlation between the disease history (epilepsy onset and total numbers of seizures) and the neuron morphology.
source: Furthermore, we recently have shown that there is no correlation between the disease history (epilepsy onset and total numbers of seizures) and the neuron morphology (Mohan et al., 2015).
evidence: Reference to previous analysis of the same patient population

claim: There is no comprehensive comparative study for assessing the value of Cm in other large brains, e.g., those of non-human primates.
source: Unfortunately, we do not yet have a comprehensive comparative study for assessing the value of Cm in other large brains, e.g., those of non-human primates.
evidence: Statement of limitation in current knowledge

claim: Recent compartmental models of pyramidal neurons in L3 of the prefrontal cortex of rhesus monkeys suggested that aged animals have smaller Cm values (~0.7 µF/cm²) than young animals (~1.1 µF/cm²).
source: Recent compartmental models of pyramidal neurons in L3 of the prefrontal cortex of rhesus monkeys suggested that aged animals have smaller Cm values (~0.7 µF/cm2) than young animals (~1.1 µF/cm2) (Rumbell et al., 2016).
evidence: Summary of findings from another study on non-human primates

claim: Further direct measurements of Cm using the nucleated patch technique in different animals could provide insights to the evolution of the specific capacitance of neuronal membranes.
source: Further direct measurements of Cm, e.g., using the nucleated patch technique in different animals, could provide insights to the evolution of the specific capacitance of neuronal membranes.
evidence: Suggestion for future research directions

claim: The specific capacitance is determined by the dielectric constant of the material composing the membrane and by the membrane thickness.
source: The specific capacitance is determined by the dielectric constant of the material composing the membrane and by the membrane thickness.
evidence: Statement based on fundamental physics principles

claim: Membrane thickness in samples from human and mouse L2/3 pyramidal cells from the temporal cortex was similar (5.1–5.8 nm).
source: We measured the membrane thickness in a few samples from human and mouse L2/3 pyramidal cells, both from the temporal cortex; both showed similar thickness of 5.1–5.8 nm (not shown).
evidence: Direct measurements of membrane thickness

claim: Gentet et al. (2000) demonstrated that transmembrane proteins have small effect on Cm.
source: Gentet et al. (2000) demonstrated that transmembrane proteins have small effect on Cm.
evidence: Summary of findings from previous study

claim: Cm of condensed phosphatidylcholine-based monolayers is sensitive to their lipid composition and molecular arrangement.
source: However, a recent study showed that Cm of condensed phosphatidylcholine-based monolayers is sensitive to their lipid composition and molecular arrangement (Lecompte et al., 2015).
evidence: Summary of findings from previous study

claim: Szoboszlay et al. (2016) showed that Cm increases significantly (from 1 µF/cm² to more than 2 µF/cm²) after adding Mefloquine to the bath in mouse cerebellar neurons.
source: Furthermore, Szoboszlay et al. (2016), using nucleated patch experiments on mouse cerebellar neurons, showed that Cm increases significantly (from 1 µF/cm2 to more than 2 µF/cm2) after adding Mefloquine to the bath
evidence: Summary of experimental findings from previous study

claim: Mefloquine is known to bind to the membrane phospholipids.
source: Mefloquine is known to bind to the membrane phospholipids (Chevli and Fitch, 1982).
evidence: Statement of established biochemical knowledge

claim: Bozek et al. (2015) showed a significant difference in the lipidome of human, chimpanzee, macaque, and mouse.
source: Interestingly, (Bozek et al., 2015) showed a significant difference in the lipidome of human, chimpanzee, macaque, and mouse.
evidence: Summary of findings from comparative lipidomics study

claim: Moschetta et al. (2005) and Chan et al. (2012) showed differences in the ratio between phospholipids, cholesterol, and sphingomyelin in human vs. rodents.
source: More specifically, Moschetta et al. (2005) and Chan et al. (2012) showed differences in the ratio between phospholipids, cholesterol, and sphingomyelin in human vs. rodents.
evidence: Summary of findings from comparative lipid composition studies

claim: The lipid composition of HL2/3 membrane explains their low Cm.
source: In view of the above studies, we suggest that the lipid composition of HL2/3 membrane explains their low Cm.
evidence: Hypothesis proposed based on integration of multiple literature findings

claim: The assertion that lipid composition explains low Cm requires direct examination of the human membranes at the molecular level.
source: This assertion requires direct examination of the human membranes at the molecular level, which is beyond the scope of the present study.
evidence: Acknowledgment of limitation and need for future work

claim: The low Cm effectively enhances signal transfer (both synaptic and action potentials).
source: Whatever the reason, the low Cm effectively enhances signal transfer (both synaptic and action potentials, Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1)
evidence: Summary of functional implications demonstrated in modeling

claim: Low Cm increases the neuron's excitability, so that less depolarizing charge is required for generating Na+ spikes.
source: and increases the neuron's excitability, so that less depolarizing charge is required for generating Na+ spikes and for supporting dendritic backpropagating Na+ action potentials (Stuart and Sakmann, 1994).
evidence: Inference from modeling results with reference to previous work on backpropagating action potentials

claim: The distinctive biophysical membrane properties of pyramidal neurons in human evolved as an outcome of evolutionary pressure.
source: We conclude by suggesting that the distinctive biophysical membrane properties of pyramidal neurons in human evolved as an outcome of evolutionary pressure
evidence: Speculative evolutionary interpretation of the findings

claim: The distinctive biophysical membrane properties resulted in an efficient information transfer, counteracting the increase in size/distances in the human brain.
source: and resulted in an efficient information transfer, counteracting the increase in size/distances in the human brain.
evidence: Speculative functional interpretation connecting membrane properties to brain scaling

claim: All procedures on human tissue were performed with the approval of the Medical Ethical Committee (METc) of the VU University Medical Centre.
source: All procedures on human tissue were performed with the approval of the Medical Ethical Committee (METc) of the VU University Medical Centre (VUmc), with written informed consent by patients involved to use brain tissue removed for the treatment of their disease for scientific research, and in accordance with Dutch license procedures and the declaration of Helsinki (VUmc METc approval 'kenmerk 2012/362').
evidence: Statement of ethical approval

claim: Slices of human temporal cortex were cut from neocortical tissue that had to be removed to enable the surgical treatment of deeper brain structures for epilepsy or tumors.
source: Slices of human temporal cortex were cut from neocortical tissue that had to be removed to enable the surgical treatment of deeper brain structures for epilepsy or tumors.
evidence: Description of tissue source

claim: Patients were 32–43 years of age.
source: Patients (32–43 years of age) provided written informed consent prior to surgery.
evidence: Demographic information about patient population

claim: In all patients, the resected neocortical tissue was located outside the epileptic focus or tumor, and displayed no structural/functional abnormalities in preoperative MRI investigations.
source: In all patients, the resected neocortical tissue was located outside the epileptic focus or tumor, and displayed no structural/functional abnormalities in preoperative MRI investigations.
evidence: Description of tissue selection criteria and quality control
